# proofread

Correct the mechanical language errors in one supplied Text Artifact, and change nothing else about it.

Run `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1 uv run "$HERE/scripts/invoke.py"` — `$HERE` is the directory that holds this SKILL.md — with everything the user typed after `/proofread`, verbatim and however many lines, on stdin. Exit 0: do what it prints. Any other exit: show what it printed to the user verbatim, and stop.

Run every UV command in this Skill with a fresh private directory as `TMPDIR`, and remove that directory after the command, including when it fails. The private directory belongs to that one command and no other run, so cleanup removes only files this run created.

A model-invoked run changes only how the Skill starts. Once started, it takes the specific Text Artifact the current turn identifies as the omitted operand and enters the same numbered steps as invocation by name. The paths join before loading any language or editorial resource; the trigger wording is not a second source of rules or an alternate execution path.

Where no Formal Invocation carries an Output Target, settle it from the current turn before correcting or writing. An unnamed destination resolves to the response, and a file mentioned only as the location of the errors names no destination: the verbs *fix* and *correct* apply to the named errors, not to the file containing them. Thus `Fix the spelling and grammar mistakes in case.md` delivers to the response. A turn that explicitly names the response or a path other than the source as the destination selects that Output Target; for example, `Write the corrected text to corrected.md` selects corrected.md as a separate Output Target. A turn that asks for the file itself to be changed selects In-place Editing only when it explicitly names that file as the object of the change or as the destination of the corrected text; for example, `Update case.md with the grammar corrections` selects In-place Editing. It remains subject to every refusal that editing mode already carries, including inline text, a URL, an uploaded or read-only source, more than one text, and a simultaneous separate Output Target. A request to save, apply, or persist the corrections without naming where they go is materially ambiguous about the destination: `Fix the grammar errors in case.md and save the corrections` asks which destination the caller intends and writes nothing. For that case and any other material ambiguity about the destination, ask which destination the caller intends and write nothing.

## Arguments

The operand is the Text Artifact: inline text, one local path, or one URL, and exactly one of them — several paths, a glob reaching more than one file, or a directory of texts is more than one. Where the invocation carries no operand, it is the single text the current turn identifies.

`--language=<language>` names the language or locale whose mechanics apply. Any spelling the Collection's resolver reaches is accepted — a canonical code (`sv`, `en_GB`), a case or separator variant of one (`en-GB`, `EN_GB`), a curated alias (`BrE`, `brittisk engelska`), or an ordinary description of a language in any language.

`--output=response|<path>` names the Output Target. `response` is the default and the value `response` states it explicitly; anything else is one filesystem path. It and In-place Editing name two destinations for one text, which is why no form carries both.

`--in-place[=<value>]` selects In-place Editing. It accepts `yes`, `on`, and `true` against `no`, `off`, and `false`; bare `--in-place` means `on`, `--in-place=off` has the same effect as omitting the option, and the default is `off`.

## Steps

1. Settle the single Text Artifact and the options from the JSON. A value outside what `## Arguments` admits — `--in-place` outside its vocabulary, or more than one Text Artifact — is refused as `$LIBRARY/references/invocation-envelope.md` says: correct nothing, write nothing, and stop. Done when one Text Artifact and a valid set of options are in hand, or you have stopped.
2. Settle the destination before anything is corrected, following `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`. Make every refusal that contract names by reading alone — In-place Editing together with a separate Output Target, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing against inline text or a URL or a source that is not a writable local file, and a destination whose parent directory does not exist — so that a refusal has nothing written behind it. Done when the destination is settled, or you have stopped.
3. Read the Text Artifact's leading YAML frontmatter where it has any, and look in it for one top-level `kntnt` map. That map is the only Kntnt configuration a document carries; `language`, `lang`, `genre`, `technique`, and every other key outside it are the document's own fields, whatever they are named and whatever they hold. Read `language` out of the map and nothing else out of it. The map is never required: a Text Artifact carrying none is proofread exactly like one that carries a complete one, its absence refusing nothing and leaving the language to the levels below it in step 4. Done when the artifact's recognized language value is known to be present, absent, or unreachable.
4. Resolve the language, taking the first of these that answers: the `--language` value; the recognized `kntnt` map's `language` value from step 3; the current Contextual Instruction; applicable Conversation Context; then the language of the Text Artifact itself, which is what inference reads and what the default already is. Suppression is that precedence working rather than an error: a Contextual Instruction every higher level has already settled leaves nothing for it to settle, and the run continues rather than refusing it as unaddressable guidance. Where saying so is useful, the delivery names the suppressed instruction beside the resolved configuration. Where that language is materially ambiguous or mixed — no dominant language, or alternation inside paragraphs — ask which language to proofread in rather than choosing one. Nothing has been written yet, so asking costs nothing to undo. Done when exactly one selector is in hand, or you have asked.
5. If step 3 found a recognized `kntnt` map whose `language` value no installed resource answers to, and `--language` supplied no value, report it as unusable artifact metadata: name the value, say that it is neither a canonical code nor an installed alias, and stop. Do not read it as the code it resembles. A `--language` value settles the parameter and suppresses this, the unusable map then being none of the run's business. Done when the run has stopped, or the metadata is not in the way.
6. Run `uv run --no-cache --no-project "$LIBRARY/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=mechanics "<selector>"`. Exit 0: take the reported `code` as the resolved language and the `mechanics` scope as this run's language-specific rules. A non-zero exit means the selector reached no single installed resource — interpret the human description semantically, propose one candidate from `uv run --no-cache --no-project "$LIBRARY/scripts/languages.py" list`, and verify it through the same `resolve` command; ask only where no unique installed candidate can be established. Then load `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/mechanics.md`, the shared mechanics contract, which holds the rules of objective correctness that do not depend on the language; it and the resolved scope together are this run's rules, and the scope is the more specific of the two wherever they meet. That one document is the whole of what is admitted from the Collection's editorial resources: load no base contract, no genre, no technique, and no anti-slop catalogue, load no other scope, and read no composition, review, or anti-slop guidance from anywhere. Done when the contract and the mechanics scope are both in hand, or you have stopped.
7. Correct every objective mechanical error in the resolved language, reading the text yourself: misspellings, grammatical errors, punctuation errors, agreement between subject and verb or noun and modifier, wrong inflection, a duplicated word, a word plainly missing, and the locale's own conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation as the mechanics scope states them, together with everything the shared mechanics contract holds. Correct all of them — a mechanical pass that leaves mechanical errors behind is a pass the user has to make again. Before this step is done, make an agreement-only re-read of every ordinary-prose sentence after the other corrections. Check agreement in both directions between subject and verb and between noun and modifier; in Swedish, `olika bild` must become `olika bilder`. Make that same re-read whether `--language` named the language or another level of the precedence settled it. A resolved locale establishes its date conventions but not what ambiguous source fields meant: `3/4` stays exactly `3/4` under both `en_GB` and `en_US` unless the Text Artifact itself establishes one reading; never expand or reorder it solely from locale. A grammatically valid word-as-word phrase such as `the word probably` remains unmarked: add no quotation marks or other emphasis unless the loaded rules identify an objective error. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Introduce no spellchecker, grammar service, or scanner of your own; the resolver above is the only script this Skill runs. Done when the mechanical errors you can identify are corrected.
8. Change nothing else. Wording, meaning, tone, register, argument, structure, factual content, formatting and markup, code and its contents, links, and metadata all come through untouched, and the frontmatter comes through byte for byte — a language value you were entitled to read is read and left exactly where it is, no `kntnt` map is added or removed, and nothing is reordered. A preference is not an error, and the rules step 6 put in hand are what says which is which: what neither of them names as an error comes through untouched, however tempting it is, and what either of them does name is corrected however deliberate it looks. A sentence improved here is the failure this Skill exists to prevent: mechanical correction was requested, and mechanical correction is the whole of what is delivered. Done when the diff you are about to deliver is mechanical throughout.
9. Deliver by `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`: the complete Text Artifact to the settled Output Target, the source file replaced where In-place Editing was requested, and a derived filename with its collisions resolved where the target is a directory. On a response target, remove every artifact or scratch file this run created and base the delivery account on the filesystem state that remains after cleanup. Where nothing was corrected and the destination is the response or the source file itself, write nothing at all and return only the short no-change status, in the language of the Text Artifact. Done when the Text Artifact has been delivered, or the no-change status has been reported.

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

# Elm Quay finds value in one view of repair reports

Elm Quay Housing’s maintenance team tested a shared repair log in two buildings to help staff on different shifts see the same information. Supervisor Maya Lind valued the shared view, but her assessment came with a reservation: she would allow more preparation time before repeating the trial.

*Published by Svale Systems.*

Elm Quay manages 640 apartments. In September 2025, its maintenance team decided to trial a shared log after storing telephone reports and emails separately. The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair.

“We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log,” Lind said in an email interview.

The maintenance team designed the categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents. Svale configured the log and trained six staff members over two sessions. For Lind, the experience offered a preparation lesson:

“We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay’s internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, recorded 31 repair reports, excluding emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

The median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, compared with three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. These figures concern assignment, not completion; there are no measurements of repair completion time, costs, or resident satisfaction.

Lind gave a qualified endorsement of repeating the trial:

“I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

The trial has not yet expanded. The team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs. Lind’s willingness to repeat the trial is her assessment of Elm Quay’s experience, not a recommendation of Svale for every housing company.

For an optional next step, read [Svale’s implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).
